title: Why You Can't Tickle Yourself
hook_promise: Why does your own touch never tickle, when someone else's does?

hook_options.line: I can't tickle myself. Here's why.
hook_options.frame_one: Host stands in a sunlit bedroom, poking own ribs with a puzzled frown while a flat gray cloud floats beside.
hook_options.answer: The brain predicts its own touch and turns it down, so there is no gap to feel.
hook_options.loop_line: Touch from someone else gets through. Me? I still can't tickle myself.

hook_options.line: Why does my own touch feel like nothing?
hook_options.frame_one: Host pokes own ribs with a deadpan face in a bedroom while a small gray cloud hovers over the finger.
hook_options.answer: The brain predicts self-made touch from the movement and dials it down.
hook_options.loop_line: So that's why my own touch feels like nothing.

hook_options.line: Your brain is cheating at tickling.
hook_options.frame_one: Host squints suspiciously at their own finger, an inch from their ribs, in a golden bedroom.
hook_options.answer: The brain predicts the touch from the movement and dulls it before it arrives.
hook_options.loop_line: Yep, my brain cheats. That's why I can't tickle myself.

storylines.title: I Tried to Tickle Myself and My Brain Said No
storylines.hook: I can't tickle myself. Here's why.
storylines.pitch: The host pokes their own ribs and feels nothing, then tries harder, but the touch stays dull. The twist: the brain predicts your own touch and turns it down, and the more a touch differs from the prediction, the more ticklish it feels. Add a delay and the tickle comes back, though with practice the brain even learns to dull the delayed touch.
storylines.conflict: The host wants to tickle themself and every attempt feels like nothing.
storylines.stakes: Each harder, faster, sneakier attempt fails, until the host suspects their own brain is working against them.
storylines.twist: The brain predicts the touch from the motor command and dials it down, and a bigger gap between the prediction and the real touch feels more ticklish.
storylines.payoff: The brain can't be surprised by its own touch, so it can't tickle you, and that is the answer to the hook.
visuals: Host pokes own ribs in a painted bedroom, a flat gray 'nothing' cloud appears
Close-up of the host's finger and ribs, tries again with a frown
Split screen: own touch (dim) vs. touch from someone else (bright)
Host holds a feather on a stick, a delay clock ticks between the move and the touch
Camera pushes in on the host's head as a small 'prediction' note glows

storylines.title: What If Your Brain Stopped Predicting Your Own Touch?
storylines.hook: What if your brain stopped predicting you?
storylines.pitch: Imagine your brain stopped cancelling the touch you cause yourself. Your own touch would feel like it came from outside, and the bigger the gap between prediction and touch, the more ticklish it feels. In reality the brain's forward model quietly mutes your own touch, and when that mechanism is abnormal, it is linked to hallucinations and passivity experiences.
storylines.conflict: The brain has to tell touch you cause apart from touch that comes from the world.
storylines.stakes: Step by step: without the prediction, your touch isn't muted, it feels more ticklish, and then your own actions start to feel like someone else's.
storylines.twist: Evidence links an abnormal predictive mechanism to auditory hallucinations and passivity experiences.
storylines.payoff: Back to reality: your brain predicts your own touch and turns it down, which is why you can't tickle yourself.
visuals: Host in a painted room switches off a glowing 'prediction' lamp
Close-up of the host's hand touching their arm, the touch drawn as a loud spark
Split screen: what if (spark) vs. what really happens (dim glow)
Host points at a painted head with a small 'forward model' note, then flips the lamp back on

storylines.title: The Case of the Tickle That Never Comes
storylines.hook: Who's stopping you from tickling yourself?
storylines.pitch: Your own touch barely registers, while the same touch from someone else lights up your brain. Clue by clue: the touch areas are quieter, the cerebellum is less active during a self-made touch, and the thalamus and touch cortices track the cerebellum only for self-touch. The culprit is a forward model that predicts the touch and mutes it.
storylines.conflict: The same touch feels ticklish from someone else but not from you, and nobody knows what is blocking it.
storylines.stakes: Each clue narrows the suspects from the whole brain to the touch cortex, the cerebellum, and finally one prediction.
storylines.twist: The cerebellum was quieter during the movement that made the touch, yet its activity still tracked other touch areas only when the touch was self-produced.
storylines.payoff: The culprit is the forward model, which predicts the touch from your own motor command and attenuates it.
visuals: Host as a detective in a painted room, a 'case file' with a feather clipped to it
Close-up of a painted brain scan with the touch cortex glowing brighter for an outside touch
Split screen: touch from outside (bright) vs. self-made touch (dim)
Map-style painted brain with pins on the cerebellum, thalamus and touch cortex
Camera push-in as the host points at the 'prediction' pin and reveals it
